screens.title: Continuous Integration and Deployment (CI/CD)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we bring together version control, automated testing, and deployment automation into a single practice called CI/CD. You will learn why teams merge frequently, how automation catches integration problems early, what it means to be release-ready, and when production releases can be fully automated. We'll use Java examples and a Maven build to make these ideas concrete. Start by thinking of integration as a daily safety check that keeps the main branch healthy. Then we expand that safety net into packaging artifacts and deploying them to staging, and finally, if your automation and monitoring are strong enough, to production directly. Along the way you'll learn how build tools, test frameworks, artifact repositories, and deployment steps fit together. This orientation matters because CI/CD is not just a set of tools — it's a discipline that reduces risk and shortens feedback loops. By the end you will be able to describe the pipeline stages for a Java project, explain the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment, and recognize the guards and signals you need before automating production releases. Consider how your team could gain faster feedback and fewer integration surprises by making integration continuous — what would change in your workflow?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Introduction to CI/CD
Continuous Integration & Deployment
Automating Java builds, tests, artifacts and releases to reduce risk and shorten feedback loops.
In this lesson
Why CI reduces integration pain and how pipelines enforce quality.
Who benefits
Developers, testers, and ops teams that want safe, frequent releases.

Source
Developer commits trigger the pipeline.

Compile, run unit and integration tests.
Artifact

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these modules you will have four practical outcomes that map to everyday development tasks. First, you will understand the core principles and benefits of Continuous Integration: why frequent merges and automated builds reduce integration pain and how immediate feedback prevents long debugging sessions. Imagine a small team pushing daily and seeing failing tests within minutes. Second, you will be able to distinguish Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment, explaining when to keep a human gate and when safe automation is appropriate. Third, you will identify the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline for Java applications — source, build with Maven or Gradle, automated tests with JUnit, artifact creation, and deployment — and explain the role of each stage. Fourth, you will explore tools and practices used to automate these stages and the importance of monitoring the deployed application. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters: shorter lead times, higher confidence, and faster recovery. Consider how these skills could change the lifecycle of a feature in your next project.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Learning Objectives
01
Understand CI principles
Learn the practice of frequent merges and automated builds that catch integration issues early. This reduces long, error-prone merge cycles and keeps the main branch releasable.
Mnemonic: small, frequent commits = small, fixable failures. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Differentiate Delivery & Deployment

Identify pipeline stages for Java
Map source, build with Maven/Gradle, run JUnit tests, create artifacts, and deploy. Know what each stage verifies and why it matters for reliability.
Mnemonic: Source → Build → Test → Artifact → Deploy. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Use tools and monitoring
Explore common CI servers, artifact repositories, and monitoring stacks. Learn why metrics and logs close the feedback loop after deployment.
Mnemonic: Build, Observe, Improve. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's frame these objectives as hands-on outcomes you can use in the next sprint. First, understanding CI means you can configure a repository hook or CI job to run a build and test on each push, and respond to a failed build by fixing it immediately. A concrete example is configuring GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to run a Maven build on pull requests. Second, distinguishing Delivery from Deployment means you can design pipelines that either stop at a staging push for manual approval, or automatically roll out small changes to production. A useful rule: use manual gates for high blast-radius changes, automated deployment for low-risk, well-tested changes. Third, mapping pipeline stages means you can write a simple script or pipeline file that runs mvn clean install, stores the resulting JAR, and triggers deployment to staging. Fourth, using monitoring and feedback means you will wire logs and metrics from production back into alerts, so failed deployments are detected quickly and rolled back if needed. These outcomes tie practical checks to the objectives and prepare you for the hands-on Maven demo that follows.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Objectives — Apply
01 — Configure CI jobs
Set up repository hooks to run builds and tests on each push. For Java, the job runs mvn clean install and reports failures immediately so you can fix them before merging.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
02 — Design gates
Choose manual approval for high-impact releases and automatic rollout for small, well-tested changes. Document who approves and why.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Store built JARs or container images in a repository so deployments use immutable, versioned artifacts instead of rebuilding on deploy.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Wire logs, metrics, and alerts to detect regressions quickly. A green pipeline alone is not enough without post-deploy observability.

screens.title: What is Continuous Integration (CI)?
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration is a development practice where developers frequently merge their code into a shared repository and each merge triggers an automated build and test process. Practically, this means teams commit small, incremental changes several times a day instead of long-lived branches. The CI server compiles the code and runs unit and integration tests immediately, producing fast feedback. A concrete example is a team that uses Git: each pull request runs an automated pipeline that executes mvn clean install and runs JUnit tests. If tests fail, the pipeline marks the build broken and notifies the author, so the problem is addressed right away. A common misconception is that CI is only a tool or server. In reality, it is a discipline combining frequent commits, reliable tests, and a culture that prioritizes fixing broken builds. Another pitfall is ignoring failing builds; CI only helps if the team treats the main branch as sacrosanct and repairs breaks quickly. Key takeaway: CI reduces integration risk by turning large merges into many small, verifiable steps. Ask yourself: how often does your team merge, and how fast do you get test results?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is CI?
Definition and developer workflow
CI means frequent merges into a central repository and an automated job that builds and runs tests on each change. The pipeline enforces quick feedback and keeps the main branch healthy.
  • • Developers push small increments multiple times per day.
  • • A CI server runs compilation, unit tests, and integration tests automatically.
  • • Failures mark the build as broken and notify the team for immediate repair.
Common mistake
Treating CI as optional or ignoring failing builds undermines the practice. The main branch must be fixed promptly for CI to work.
Key Takeaway

CI provides fast feedback on integration problems by running automated builds and tests on every merge.

Concrete example: Pull request CI
A pull request triggers a pipeline that runs mvn clean install, runs JUnit tests, and returns pass/fail. If tests fail, the author fixes the issue before merging.
Process
  1. Developer creates a short-lived branch and commits small changes.
  2. Push triggers CI job: checkout, build, test, static analysis.
  3. Pipeline reports results; green means merge, red means fix and rerun.
Analogy
Think of CI like continuous spell-check for code: it highlights problems immediately so they never accumulate into a hard-to-fix mess.

screens.title: Typical CI/CD Pipeline Stages
screens.narratorSegment: A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of automated stages that starts when code is pushed to version control and ends when an artifact reaches a target environment. The Source stage simply records the commit and triggers the pipeline. The Build stage compiles source code and resolves dependencies — for Java that typically means running a Maven or Gradle build to create class files. Next, the Test stage executes automated unit and integration tests with frameworks like JUnit and Mockito. Tests should run fast and cover critical paths; missing integration tests is a common reason bugs only show up after manual staging. After tests pass, the Artifact stage packages the application into a versioned unit such as a JAR or Docker image and stores it in a repository like Nexus or Artifactory. Finally, the Deploy stage installs the artifact into staging or production. Deployments may be automated or gated by manual approvals depending on risk. A concrete example: a push triggers a pipeline that runs mvn clean install, executes JUnit tests, creates a JAR and uploads it to an artifact repo, and then a deployment job copies the JAR to a staging server. Misconception: a green build guarantees correctness — it only guarantees that the tests you ran passed. Always ask: which tests are missing, and how quickly can we detect regression in production?

keyIdea.text: Each stage has a clear responsibility: source triggers, build compiles, tests verify, artifact packages, and deploy delivers — gaps in tests or artifacts create blind spots.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Pipeline Stages
Pipeline steps
Source
Triggers pipeline on push or PR.
Build
Compile and resolve dependencies (Maven/Gradle).
Test
Run unit, integration, and acceptance tests (JUnit, Mockito).
Artifact
Package JAR/WAR or Docker image and publish to a repo.
Deploy
Install to staging or production; may include manual gate.
Supporting explanation
  • • Build must be deterministic so artifacts are repeatable.
  • • Tests should include fast unit tests plus selective integration tests in the pipeline.
  • • Artifacts provide immutability: the deployed artifact is identical to the one tested.
Concrete scenario
A developer pushes to main; CI runs mvn clean install, tests pass, pipeline creates example-app-1.0.jar, stores it in Nexus, and a deploy job copies it to staging for QA.
Misconception
Green pipeline does not guarantee full correctness if critical tests are missing. Increase coverage and add integration checks where needed.
Key Takeaway

Each pipeline stage verifies a distinct property: source triggers, build produces binaries, tests validate behavior, artifacts are immutable, and deploys deliver to environments.

screens.title: Build and Test with Maven
screens.narratorSegment: For Java projects, build automation is often handled by Maven or Gradle. Maven defines project structure, dependencies, and test plugins in a pom. xml. A CI job usually executes a single command such as mvn clean install which cleans previous outputs, compiles the source, runs JUnit tests, and packages the application into a JAR or WAR. The pom. xml also declares test dependencies like JUnit, and configures plugins such as the surefire plugin for running tests. A concrete example is provided in the course material: the pom snippet includes compiler settings and JUnit dependencies. In a CI server, the build step runs automatically on each push; if mvn clean install fails, the pipeline stops and the build is marked failed. A common misconception is that a successful build guarantees behavior in production — it guarantees only that the compiled code passed the configured tests. Make sure your test suite includes integration tests for system interactions where necessary. Key takeaway: keep your pom accurate, run mvn clean install in CI, and ensure tests are reliable and fast so pipelines complete quickly and give useful feedback.

keyIdea.title: Maven in CI
keyIdea.text: Use mvn clean install to compile, test, and package. Configure dependencies and test plugins in pom.xml so CI reproduces local builds consistently.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Maven Build Walkthrough
Example pom.xml (snippet)
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>com.cohortia</groupId>
    <artifactId>simple-java-app</artifactId>
    <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.source>11</maven.compiler.source>
        <maven.compiler.target>11</maven.compiler.target>
        <junit.version>5.10.0</junit.version>
    </properties>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter-api</artifactId>
            <version>${junit.version}</version>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.8.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <source>${maven.compiler.source}</source>
                    <target>${maven.compiler.target}</target>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.0.0-M5</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
A CI server runs mvn clean install, which executes the lifecycle above to produce a test-verified artifact. Keep versions and plugins consistent between local and CI environments.
Terminal demo (conceptual)
$ mvn clean install
[INFO] Scanning for projects...
[INFO] ---------------------
[INFO] --- maven-compiler-plugin:3.8.1:compile (default-compile) @ simple-java-app ---
[INFO] --- maven-surefire-plugin:3.0.0-M5:test (default-test) @ simple-java-app ---
[INFO] Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
If tests fail, the build exits non-zero and CI marks the job failed. Keep tests fast and deterministic so pipelines remain responsive.
Pro Tip

Pin plugin and dependency versions to ensure CI builds match local builds.

screens.title: Continuous Delivery vs. Continuous Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment are closely related steps on the same automation spectrum, but they answer different operational questions. Continuous Delivery means your pipeline builds, tests, and packages every change so that the result is always in a deployable state. The final push to production remains a human decision or gated approval. Continuous Deployment takes one more step: every change that passes the pipeline is automatically released to production without a manual gate. A concrete example for a Java team: with Continuous Delivery, a build produces a JAR and deploys it automatically to staging for acceptance testing; a product manager then approves the release to production. With Continuous Deployment, that approval is replaced by an automated promotion and rollout to production after the same automated checks pass. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment removes safety. It does not if you design strong tests, feature flags, and rollback paths. The takeaway is practical: choose Continuous Delivery when you need controlled releases, and adopt Continuous Deployment when your automation and monitoring are mature enough to safely reduce human steps. Which approach matches your risk profile and release cadence?

keyIdea.title: Manual gate vs. automatic release
keyIdea.text: Continuous Delivery keeps software always ready to release; Continuous Deployment removes the manual release step and deploys every successful change.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Continuous Delivery vs Deployment
Continuous Delivery
Always ready to release
Software is built, tested, packaged, and deployed to staging automatically. Production release requires a human decision.
CD
Continuous Deployment
Automated production release
Every change that passes automated gates is released to production automatically, relying on tests and monitoring for safety.
CD+
Key Takeaway

Pick Continuous Delivery when human approval is required. Move to Continuous Deployment when tests, feature flags, and monitoring give you fast, safe rollbacks.

Side-by-side comparison
Release Control
Manual gate for production
Release Control
Fully automated promotion to production
Risk
Lower blast radius via human checks
Speed
Faster time to user when automated safely
Concrete example
Continuous Delivery scenario
A Maven build produces a JAR, automated tests run, artifact is deployed to staging, and a release manager triggers production when ready.
Continuous Deployment scenario
The same pipeline includes automated acceptance tests and monitoring checks, and passing changes roll out to production automatically using phased rollouts.
Common misconception: Continuous Deployment is reckless. In practice it requires stronger tests and rollout strategies.

screens.title: Artifacts and Repositories
screens.narratorSegment: An artifact is the packaged output of your build: a JAR, WAR, or container image that can be deployed. Artifact creation is an explicit stage in a CI/CD pipeline. For Java projects, tools like Maven or Gradle compile code, run tests, and then package the application into an artifact file. That artifact is often pushed to a repository such as Nexus or Artifactory so teams and deployment systems can pull a single authoritative binary. Storing artifacts centrally prevents rebuilds during deployment and ensures traceability of exact versions in production. A concrete example: after a successful build, the pipeline stores simple-java-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT. jar in an artifact repository and records version metadata. When a deployment job runs, it fetches that exact JAR to deploy to staging or production. Common mistakes are rebuilding from source at deploy time or not storing build metadata, which makes rollbacks and audits hard. Key practices include immutable artifacts, semantic versioning or unique build identifiers, and retention policies in your repository. Think of artifacts as the single source of truth for releases; if you can pull the exact artifact later, you can reliably reproduce or roll back the deployed state.

keyIdea.title: Immutable artifacts for reliable deployments
keyIdea.text: Create and store deployable artifacts in a central repository so deployments use exact, versioned binaries rather than rebuilds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Artifacts & Repos
Artifact creation steps
  1. Source pushed to VCS triggers pipeline.
  2. Build tool compiles and runs tests.
  3. Packaging produces JAR/WAR or container image.
  4. Artifact is published to a repository with metadata.
Repository roles
  • Store immutable binaries for repeatable deploys.
  • Provide access controls and retention policies.
  • Serve as an audit trail for released versions.
Examples: Nexus, Artifactory. Keep credentials secure when publishing artifacts.
Visual: artifact lifecycle
Build
Compile and test to produce a versioned binary.
Package
Package into a JAR/WAR or container image with metadata.
Publish
Upload to a repository for deployment and traceability.
Concrete example
After tests pass, the CI job stores simple-java-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar in the artifact repository and records the build number. The deploy job later fetches that JAR by exact name to ensure the same binary is deployed to staging and production.
Key Takeaway

Treat artifacts as immutable single sources of truth. Publish them with version metadata to enable reliable deploys and rollbacks.

screens.title: Deployment Strategies for Java Applications
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is the step that moves an artifact into an environment where users or systems interact with it. For Java applications you have several practical strategies. The simplest is copying a JAR to a server and restarting the JVM process. Containerizing the app in a Docker image brings environment consistency and makes it easier to run in orchestration platforms. Kubernetes provides rolling updates, replica management, and integration with service discovery. Serverless platforms can be used for specific functions where packaging into an artifact or container is replaced by a function deployment. Rollout patterns matter: blue/green keeps two parallel environments and switches traffic to the new one after validation. Canary rollouts send a subset of traffic to the new release to observe behavior before full promotion. The choice depends on your architecture and risk tolerance. An example: a team packages a microservice into a container and performs a canary release on Kubernetes, monitoring latency and error rate. If metrics remain healthy, they promote the image. A misconception is that containers solve all problems; they help with consistency but require orchestration, proper image management, and monitoring. The core idea: match deployment technique to application needs and ensure you can control blast radius and roll back safely.

keyIdea.text: From JAR copy to canary on Kubernetes, choose the deployment approach that balances speed, observability, and rollback capability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Deployment Strategies
Strategy cards
JAR copy & restart
Simple, low tooling. Suitable for small services but fragile at scale.
Container image
Encapsulates runtime and dependencies for consistent deployments.
Kubernetes rolling/canary
Orchestrator supports phased rollouts and automated scaling for microservices.
Serverless
Function deployments for event-oriented workloads, reducing server management work.
Rollout patterns
Blue/Green
Switch all traffic to a validated new environment, fallback by switching back.
Canary
Route a fraction of traffic to observe behavior before full rollout.
Rolling update
Replace instances incrementally with the new version to avoid downtime.
Immutable deployments
Deploy new instances instead of modifying running ones to simplify rollback.
Concrete scenario
A microservice is containerized, pushed to an image registry, and deployed to Kubernetes. The team performs a canary release, watches latency and error metrics, then promotes to full production if stable.
Misconception: containers automatically make deployments safe. They help, but you still need rollout and monitoring strategies.

screens.title: Monitoring and Feedback Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring and feedback are the safety net that makes CI/CD practical. After deployment you must observe logs, metrics, and error rates continuously so that regressions surface quickly. Logs provide diagnostic detail, metrics reveal trends like latency and throughput, and alerts notify teams when thresholds are crossed. Tools mentioned in the chapter include Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and dashboards, the ELK stack for log aggregation, and cloud services such as CloudWatch or Azure Monitor. A concrete example: if a new deployment increases error rate by a measurable amount, alerting should trigger rollbacks or a canary halt and notify the responsible engineers. A common misconception is that monitoring is only for production; instrumenting staging and canary environments produces faster, safer releases. Effective feedback loops also include reporting build and test failures back into the developer workflow so issues are fixed quickly. Finally, monitoring supports automated responses: a health check failure can trigger a redeploy or a rollback to a known good artifact. The essential idea is that fast, reliable observability converts automated deployments from risky to manageable. Monitoring and Feedback Loops means collect logs and metrics, set meaningful alerts, and route feedback to development so issues are detected and resolved rapidly.. In practical terms, from logs and metrics to fast detection and team feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Observe, alert, and close the loop
keyIdea.text: Collect logs and metrics, set meaningful alerts, and route feedback to development so issues are detected and resolved rapidly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Monitoring & Feedback
Observability stack
Logs
Detailed events for debugging. Use structured logging and aggregation.
Metrics
Numeric measures like latency and error rate for trend detection.
Traces & Dashboards
End-to-end traces and dashboards surface root causes and patterns.
Alerting rule (example)
error_rate > 1% for 5 minutes → page on-call team and halt canary rollout
Concrete case study
A canary release shows a 2x increase in request latency. Grafana dashboard highlights latency spike and ELK logs show a specific exception. The monitoring alert pauses further rollout and notifies the team. The team inspects logs, identifies a dependency regression, rolls back to the previous artifact, and observes metrics return to baseline.
Feedback loop checklist
  • Instrument code for metrics and structured logs.
  • Set meaningful thresholds and noisy-alert suppression.
  • Integrate alerts with team channels and incident playbooks.
Key Takeaway

Good monitoring turns automated deploys into safe experiments. Fast detection and clear responses keep users protected.

screens.title: Security, Rollbacks, and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Automation magnifies both your strengths and your mistakes. Security and rollback planning are essential parts of CI/CD. Never hardcode credentials such as A P I keys or database passwords in pipeline scripts or code. Use the CI/CD platform's secret store or cloud provider-managed secrets and fine-grained access controls. For rollback strategies, keep previous artifacts available in your repository and design your deployment to support quick reversion, whether by redeploying an earlier artifact, switching blue/green traffic, or aborting a canary. One of the most damaging operational mistakes is allowing the main branch to remain broken. If CI failures are ignored, integration benefits vanish. Another frequent problem is insufficient test coverage; green builds may still hide critical integration errors if integration and end-to-end tests are missing. Environment inconsistency between local, staging, and production causes 'works on my machine' surprises; use containerization or IaC to reduce drift. In practice, build automated gates, short feedback loops, and a culture that prioritizes fixing broken builds immediately. A short checklist: secure secrets, keep immutable artifacts, automate rollbacks, and make build health everyone’s responsibility. What single change could you make to reduce your deployment blast radius today?

keyIdea.title: Secure automation with safe recovery
keyIdea.text: Use secrets management, preserve old artifacts, and practice rollback patterns to limit the impact of failures.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Security & Rollbacks
Security rules
  • Never hardcode credentials in code or pipeline scripts.
  • Use CI secrets stores or cloud-managed secret services.
  • Limit access rights for pipeline service accounts.
Concrete example
Store database credentials in the CI tool's secret vault. The deployment reads them at runtime from a secure variable, not from the repository.
Rollback and readiness
Keep previous artifacts and metadata so you can redeploy a known good version quickly. Use blue/green or canary releases to limit blast radius and enable fast rollback when alerts fire.
Common mistakes
  • Ignoring failing CI builds and leaving main branch broken.
  • Insufficient automated test coverage for critical flows.
  • Environment drift between development, staging, and production.
Pro-tip

Automate short, fast checks early and prioritize fixing the main branch. Security and build health are team responsibilities, not incidental tasks.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three crucial concepts to carry forward. Continuous Integration is the discipline of frequently merging code and running automated builds and tests to find integration issues quickly. Continuous Delivery builds on that by ensuring every successful build produces a tested, deployable artifact that can be released to production at any time, typically gated by a human decision. Continuous Deployment goes further by automatically releasing every successful build to production, which demands confidence in automated tests, monitoring, and rollback mechanisms. Keep these definitions practical: CI protects integration health, Continuous Delivery guarantees readiness, and Continuous Deployment prioritizes speed with safety nets. As you adopt CI/CD, focus not only on the tools but on traceable artifacts, reliable tests, and observability. Which of these three concepts will you prioritize introducing to your team's workflow first?

keyIdea.title: CI → Delivery → Deployment
keyIdea.text: A progression from frequent integration to always-ready releases and finally to automated production releases with strong safety practices.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts
Continuous Integration (CI)
Frequent merges with automated builds and tests to catch integration errors early.
Continuous Delivery
Every build is packaged and tested so the software is always ready to release with a manual gate.
Continuous Deployment
Every successful build that passes gates is automatically released to production.
Summary

CI reduces integration risk. Continuous Delivery makes releases safe and repeatable. Continuous Deployment increases delivery speed when backed by strong tests and monitoring.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline, Artifact, Monitoring
keyIdea.text: Automate the pipeline, produce immutable artifacts, and monitor deployed systems to complete the feedback loop.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts
CI/CD Pipeline
Automated workflow from version control to deployment including build, test, and artifact stages.
Artifact
A versioned, deployable package such as a JAR, WAR, or container image stored for repeatable deploys.
Monitoring
Collect logs and metrics, set alerts, and feed results back to developers for fast remediation.
Final Takeaway

CI/CD is a cultural and technical system: automate builds and tests, produce immutable artifacts, and observe deployments so your team can release safely and often.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we bring together version control, automated testing, and deployment automation into a single practice called CI/CD. You will learn why teams merge frequently, how automation catches integration problems early, what it means to be release-ready, and when production releases can be fully automated. We'll use Java examples and a Maven build to make these ideas concrete. Start by thinking of integration as a daily safety check that keeps the main branch healthy. Then we expand that safety net into packaging artifacts and deploying them to staging, and finally, if your automation and monitoring are strong enough, to production directly. Along the way you'll learn how build tools, test frameworks, artifact repositories, and deployment steps fit together. This orientation matters because CI/CD is not just a set of tools — it's a discipline that reduces risk and shortens feedback loops. By the end you will be able to describe the pipeline stages for a Java project, explain the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment, and recognize the guards and signals you need before automating production releases. Consider how your team could gain faster feedback and fewer integration surprises by making integration continuous — what would change in your workflow?

By the end of these modules you will have four practical outcomes that map to everyday development tasks. First, you will understand the core principles and benefits of Continuous Integration: why frequent merges and automated builds reduce integration pain and how immediate feedback prevents long debugging sessions. Imagine a small team pushing daily and seeing failing tests within minutes. Second, you will be able to distinguish Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment, explaining when to keep a human gate and when safe automation is appropriate. Third, you will identify the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline for Java applications — source, build with Maven or Gradle, automated tests with JUnit, artifact creation, and deployment — and explain the role of each stage. Fourth, you will explore tools and practices used to automate these stages and the importance of monitoring the deployed application. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters: shorter lead times, higher confidence, and faster recovery. Consider how these skills could change the lifecycle of a feature in your next project.

Now let's frame these objectives as hands-on outcomes you can use in the next sprint. First, understanding CI means you can configure a repository hook or CI job to run a build and test on each push, and respond to a failed build by fixing it immediately. A concrete example is configuring GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to run a Maven build on pull requests. Second, distinguishing Delivery from Deployment means you can design pipelines that either stop at a staging push for manual approval, or automatically roll out small changes to production. A useful rule: use manual gates for high blast-radius changes, automated deployment for low-risk, well-tested changes. Third, mapping pipeline stages means you can write a simple script or pipeline file that runs mvn clean install, stores the resulting JAR, and triggers deployment to staging. Fourth, using monitoring and feedback means you will wire logs and metrics from production back into alerts, so failed deployments are detected quickly and rolled back if needed. These outcomes tie practical checks to the objectives and prepare you for the hands-on Maven demo that follows.

Continuous Integration is a development practice where developers frequently merge their code into a shared repository and each merge triggers an automated build and test process. Practically, this means teams commit small, incremental changes several times a day instead of long-lived branches. The CI server compiles the code and runs unit and integration tests immediately, producing fast feedback. A concrete example is a team that uses Git: each pull request runs an automated pipeline that executes mvn clean install and runs JUnit tests. If tests fail, the pipeline marks the build broken and notifies the author, so the problem is addressed right away. A common misconception is that CI is only a tool or server. In reality, it is a discipline combining frequent commits, reliable tests, and a culture that prioritizes fixing broken builds. Another pitfall is ignoring failing builds; CI only helps if the team treats the main branch as sacrosanct and repairs breaks quickly. Key takeaway: CI reduces integration risk by turning large merges into many small, verifiable steps. Ask yourself: how often does your team merge, and how fast do you get test results?

A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of automated stages that starts when code is pushed to version control and ends when an artifact reaches a target environment. The Source stage simply records the commit and triggers the pipeline. The Build stage compiles source code and resolves dependencies — for Java that typically means running a Maven or Gradle build to create class files. Next, the Test stage executes automated unit and integration tests with frameworks like JUnit and Mockito. Tests should run fast and cover critical paths; missing integration tests is a common reason bugs only show up after manual staging. After tests pass, the Artifact stage packages the application into a versioned unit such as a JAR or Docker image and stores it in a repository like Nexus or Artifactory. Finally, the Deploy stage installs the artifact into staging or production. Deployments may be automated or gated by manual approvals depending on risk. A concrete example: a push triggers a pipeline that runs mvn clean install, executes JUnit tests, creates a JAR and uploads it to an artifact repo, and then a deployment job copies the JAR to a staging server. Misconception: a green build guarantees correctness — it only guarantees that the tests you ran passed. Always ask: which tests are missing, and how quickly can we detect regression in production?

For Java projects, build automation is often handled by Maven or Gradle. Maven defines project structure, dependencies, and test plugins in a pom. xml. A CI job usually executes a single command such as mvn clean install which cleans previous outputs, compiles the source, runs JUnit tests, and packages the application into a JAR or WAR. The pom. xml also declares test dependencies like JUnit, and configures plugins such as the surefire plugin for running tests. A concrete example is provided in the course material: the pom snippet includes compiler settings and JUnit dependencies. In a CI server, the build step runs automatically on each push; if mvn clean install fails, the pipeline stops and the build is marked failed. A common misconception is that a successful build guarantees behavior in production — it guarantees only that the compiled code passed the configured tests. Make sure your test suite includes integration tests for system interactions where necessary. Key takeaway: keep your pom accurate, run mvn clean install in CI, and ensure tests are reliable and fast so pipelines complete quickly and give useful feedback.

Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment are closely related steps on the same automation spectrum, but they answer different operational questions. Continuous Delivery means your pipeline builds, tests, and packages every change so that the result is always in a deployable state. The final push to production remains a human decision or gated approval. Continuous Deployment takes one more step: every change that passes the pipeline is automatically released to production without a manual gate. A concrete example for a Java team: with Continuous Delivery, a build produces a JAR and deploys it automatically to staging for acceptance testing; a product manager then approves the release to production. With Continuous Deployment, that approval is replaced by an automated promotion and rollout to production after the same automated checks pass. A common misconception is that Continuous Deployment removes safety. It does not if you design strong tests, feature flags, and rollback paths. The takeaway is practical: choose Continuous Delivery when you need controlled releases, and adopt Continuous Deployment when your automation and monitoring are mature enough to safely reduce human steps. Which approach matches your risk profile and release cadence?

An artifact is the packaged output of your build: a JAR, WAR, or container image that can be deployed. Artifact creation is an explicit stage in a CI/CD pipeline. For Java projects, tools like Maven or Gradle compile code, run tests, and then package the application into an artifact file. That artifact is often pushed to a repository such as Nexus or Artifactory so teams and deployment systems can pull a single authoritative binary. Storing artifacts centrally prevents rebuilds during deployment and ensures traceability of exact versions in production. A concrete example: after a successful build, the pipeline stores simple-java-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT. jar in an artifact repository and records version metadata. When a deployment job runs, it fetches that exact JAR to deploy to staging or production. Common mistakes are rebuilding from source at deploy time or not storing build metadata, which makes rollbacks and audits hard. Key practices include immutable artifacts, semantic versioning or unique build identifiers, and retention policies in your repository. Think of artifacts as the single source of truth for releases; if you can pull the exact artifact later, you can reliably reproduce or roll back the deployed state.

Deployment is the step that moves an artifact into an environment where users or systems interact with it. For Java applications you have several practical strategies. The simplest is copying a JAR to a server and restarting the JVM process. Containerizing the app in a Docker image brings environment consistency and makes it easier to run in orchestration platforms. Kubernetes provides rolling updates, replica management, and integration with service discovery. Serverless platforms can be used for specific functions where packaging into an artifact or container is replaced by a function deployment. Rollout patterns matter: blue/green keeps two parallel environments and switches traffic to the new one after validation. Canary rollouts send a subset of traffic to the new release to observe behavior before full promotion. The choice depends on your architecture and risk tolerance. An example: a team packages a microservice into a container and performs a canary release on Kubernetes, monitoring latency and error rate. If metrics remain healthy, they promote the image. A misconception is that containers solve all problems; they help with consistency but require orchestration, proper image management, and monitoring. The core idea: match deployment technique to application needs and ensure you can control blast radius and roll back safely.

Monitoring and feedback are the safety net that makes CI/CD practical. After deployment you must observe logs, metrics, and error rates continuously so that regressions surface quickly. Logs provide diagnostic detail, metrics reveal trends like latency and throughput, and alerts notify teams when thresholds are crossed. Tools mentioned in the chapter include Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and dashboards, the ELK stack for log aggregation, and cloud services such as CloudWatch or Azure Monitor. A concrete example: if a new deployment increases error rate by a measurable amount, alerting should trigger rollbacks or a canary halt and notify the responsible engineers. A common misconception is that monitoring is only for production; instrumenting staging and canary environments produces faster, safer releases. Effective feedback loops also include reporting build and test failures back into the developer workflow so issues are fixed quickly. Finally, monitoring supports automated responses: a health check failure can trigger a redeploy or a rollback to a known good artifact. The essential idea is that fast, reliable observability converts automated deployments from risky to manageable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
